newsitem.title: JAPAN: IMF says sees no Mexico-style forex crisis in Asia.
newsitem.headline: IMF says sees no Mexico-style forex crisis in Asia.

text.p: The International Monetary Fund (IMF) does not see the emergence of a Mexico-style currency crisis in Asia, but would be ready to help if its advice or financial assistance were needed, Stanley Fischer, first deputy managing director of the IMF, said.
Fischer told Reuters Financial Television in an interview broadcast on Wednesday that most economies in the region that are said to be slowing down still have plenty of room to adjust their growth.
"They can, if they take the necessary measures in those countries that need them, get out of these problems without a great deal of social cost and damage to the economy," he said.
He was responding to a question about whether the IMF sees the possibility of a Mexico-style crisis within Asia.
Fischer said that recent coordinated intervention by Asian central banks had helped to calm volatility in regional currency markets.

"The measures that were taken in the last couple of weeks seem to have done pretty well in calming the markets. That's encouraging," he said, referring to coordinated intervention to prop up the Thai baht earlier this month.
He added that the IMF would be willing to help any nation in the region which needed advice, financial assistance or an economic reform programme with an international stamp of approval from the IMF.
"These things are not unknown in this region and if the circumstances warrant it, and if the countries want it, we would certainly be there," he said.
Fischer is in Tokyo to attend a two-day conference on macro-economic adjustment and economic growth.

On Tuesday, Deutsche Morgan Grenfell said in its weekly research report that the probability remained high that Asia may be struck by the same sort of cash and liquidity crisis which hit Mexico in 1994.
The baht and Thai stocks were hammered in the past weeks by selling triggered by a poor outlook for the once-booming economy.
The attack on the Thai baht set off coordinated intervention by the Bank of Thailand, the Monetary Authority of Singapore and other Asian central banks.
